At the end of a narrow street, between a locksmith and a shop that had been “Opening Soon” for eleven years, there was a small office where you could retrieve things you had forgotten.

Not misplaced things. No keys, no earrings, no phones.

Forgotten things.

The name of your first teacher’s dog. The tune your father hummed while washing dishes. What you had meant to say before the conversation changed.

The woman behind the counter wore green cardigans and never asked for identification.

“You’ll know if it’s yours,” she said.

Most people came once.

A man collected the smell of his grandmother’s hallway and stood very still for several minutes. A teenager recovered an elaborate game she had invented with her brother before they learned to be embarrassed by each other. Someone came for a grudge and was gently advised to browse a little longer.

One wet Thursday, a woman arrived carrying nothing.

“I think I’ve forgotten what I wanted,” she said.

The clerk looked up.

“For lunch?”

“For my life.”

“Ah.” The clerk put down her pen. “We get that.”

She disappeared through a door behind the counter. The woman heard drawers opening, a small crash, and a muttered complaint about the filing system.

At last the clerk returned with a shallow cardboard box.

Inside were a smooth stone, a photograph of a horse, three pencils, and a paper crown.

“This can’t be right,” the woman said.

“Take your time.”

She picked up the stone.

She remembered wanting to walk beside a river until she found where it began.

The horse: wanting to be trusted by something large and easily frightened.

The pencils: wanting to make pictures good enough that other people could see what she saw.

The crown embarrassed her.

“I wanted to be queen?”

“Possibly. We don’t interpret.”

Then she remembered a birthday party. She had made crowns for everyone, even the adults. Her uncle had worn his all the way home on the bus.

She turned the paper over in her hands. There was a thumbprint in the glue.

“Do people do anything with these?” she asked.

“Sometimes. One gentleman took up tap dancing. We had a complaint from his downstairs neighbour.”

The woman laughed, then put the crown back carefully.

“Can I keep the box?”

“That’s what it’s for.”

Outside, the rain had stopped. She stood beneath the office awning and looked at the time. There were emails waiting, and she needed to buy something for dinner.

The river was twenty minutes in the wrong direction.

She went to look at it.
